advisor.summary: When a renovation replaces a roof, HVAC system, windows, or another structural component, the tangible property regulations require the new component to be capitalized — while the old one's remaining basis would otherwise keep depreciating inside the building for decades. Reg. §1.168(i)-8(d)(2) provides an election to treat the retirement as a partial disposition: the replaced component's remaining adjusted basis deducts as a current loss, the related demolition and removal costs deduct under Reg. §1.263(a)-3(g)(2) rather than being capitalized, and the retired basis leaves the ledger, never to return as recapture on sale. The election has no form of its own — claiming the loss on the timely filed original return for the disposition year is the election — which makes the deadline the whole game. The engine models the retired component's remaining basis as a current rental deduction.
mechanics: The trigger is a capitalizable restoration under Reg. §1.263(a)-3(k) — the same event that puts the new component on the depreciation schedule opens the election on the old one.

The deduction equals the retired component's remaining adjusted basis; where the original cost was never separately stated, Reg. §1.168(i)-8 accepts any reasonable method, including discounting the replacement cost back to the acquisition date (a Producer Price Index rollback) and applying the depreciation already taken.
Removal and demolition costs tied to the disposed component deduct currently under Reg. §1.263(a)-3(g)(2) once a disposition loss is claimed — often worth as much as the basis loss itself.
The retired basis and its accumulated depreciation exit the fixed-asset ledger, so they never resurface as recapture on a later sale — a character benefit stacked on the timing benefit.
The election is made by reporting the loss under §165 on the timely filed original return (extensions included) for the retirement year; once that return is filed, the election is generally lost.
The model deducts the retired basis against the rental in the current year; quantified removal costs can be added to the input.

requirements: A current-year renovation retiring an identifiable building component — roof, HVAC, windows, plumbing runs, facade.
A documented, reasonable method for the retired component's remaining basis (cost records, cost segregation detail, or a PPI-discounted replacement cost).
The loss claimed on the timely filed original return for the disposition year — that filing is the election itself.
The replacement capitalized under the tangible property regulations; the election pairs with capitalization rather than replacing it.
risks: The deadline is the leading failure mode: this is an annual, return-embedded election with no standalone relief procedure, and a loss omitted from the timely original return generally stays buried in the building's basis — valuation is the exam issue, but the calendar is the malpractice issue; no marquee case exists because these fights rarely leave exam.
Guessed valuations for the old component invite adjustment; a reasonable-method computation with the math retained is the defense.
If the replacement is actually a deductible repair under the tangible property regulations, expensing usually beats the election — run the repair analysis first.
Ledger hygiene matters: the retired basis must actually come off the depreciation schedule, or the deduction double-counts.
Any loss created still runs through §469 gating for owners who lack a passive-loss path.
stateNotes: Conformity: the tangible property regulations are federal method rules, and states conform through their federal starting points — there is no separate state election.
Missouri conforms through federal AGI (RSMo §143.121), so the disposition loss reaches the Missouri return unchanged.
PTET interaction: for buildings held in an electing pass-through, the loss shrinks the PTET base in the renovation year; directly held rentals see no PTET interaction.
reviewChecklist: Renovation inventoried before filing: retired components, removal costs, and replacement capitalization all identified.
Remaining-basis computation documented under the chosen reasonable method.
Loss reported on the timely original return for the correct year — deadline verified.
Depreciation schedule updated: retired basis off, replacement on.
Repair-vs-capitalization analysis run first and the conclusion memorialized.

client.teaser: Replacing a roof or HVAC? The one you tore out still earns a deduction.
client.headline: Renovating? Deduct the piece you removed
plainEnglish: When you replace a roof or an air system on a rental building, the new one must be deducted slowly, over many years. But the old one you removed still has unused cost sitting in your tax records. Left alone, that cost keeps seeping out for decades — for a roof in a landfill.

A special election lets you deduct all of the old part's remaining cost in the year you replace it. The cost of tearing it out and hauling it away becomes deductible right away too. Together, those two pieces can add up to a large write-off.
The catch is timing. The election only works on the tax return for the renovation year. Tell us before we file, and we capture it. Tell us two years later, and it is usually gone for good.
client.analogy: It is like trade-in credit for old equipment — but the store only honors it at the register, not after you drive home.
benefits: Deduct the old component's leftover cost in the year you replace it
Demolition and removal costs become deductible right away
Cuts the tax bill when you eventually sell the building
No special application — just the right reporting, filed on time
steps: WE calculate what the removed component was still worth on paper, using accepted methods.
WE claim the loss on that year's return and tidy up your depreciation records.
WE keep the calculations and invoices as your support file.
YOU tell us about renovations in the year they happen — before we file.
clientCommitments: Report renovations in the year of the work, not at a later filing
Save contractor invoices that break out demolition and removal charges
